Chapter 8: The Cost of Belief—Families, Children, and the Toll of Devotion.
For a lot of people, this movement wasn’t just a personal journey—it became a family story. Parents brought their kids in, truly believing they were giving them a shot at happiness and a deeper sense of meaning. Over time, entire generations grew up inside the organization, their lives shaped by its routines and core beliefs.
But here’s the thing—the price of that kind of devotion could be steep. Kids were raised in a world that felt separate from everyone else. They were taught to see outsiders as dangerous, and the group itself as their real family. School sometimes took a back seat to religious lessons and work assignments. Making friends with people outside? That was discouraged, if not outright forbidden. And if a family member left the faith, staying in touch was tightly controlled.
There’s one story that really brings this to life—a boy whose parents were deeply committed to the group. He remembered feeling both special and strangely alone. His days were filled with group activities, learning the group’s language and traditions. But he missed out on those simple childhood moments—birthday parties, sleepovers, even just going to regular school events. Whenever he wondered about life outside the group, he was told the world was just full of danger and lies.
It wasn’t just the children who felt the pressure. Parents were expected to be role models—volunteering their time, their energy, and making sure their kids always followed the rules. If someone slipped up, they risked being labeled a “suppressive person.” And that label? It could mean being kicked out and losing contact with everyone you love.
The group’s policy of “disconnection” was especially tough. Members were told to cut off anyone seen as an enemy of the faith—even if it meant saying goodbye to a spouse, a child, or a parent. The emotional cost was heartbreaking. Some families were torn apart, with siblings told not to speak, and grandparents suddenly cut off from their grandchildren.
One mother shared how she’d been forced to disconnect from her daughter. She described it as a kind of grief that never quite went away. She held onto hope they’d be reunited someday, but the pain of separation was always right there. For her, even the promise of spiritual advancement just wasn’t enough to make up for what she’d lost.
Still, despite all these hardships, many families stuck together within the group. The sense of community, the shared rituals, and the belief in something bigger than themselves gave comfort and meaning to their lives. But for those who questioned the path or eventually left, the journey was often marked by loss, regret, and the tough work of rebuilding connections outside the group.
In the end, the cost of belief isn’t just about money or time—it’s about the bonds of love and trust that make life truly meaningful.
